job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Priya Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior auditor at a mid-size firm called Hartwell & Pike in Bristol, three months in. I get in at half eight, and I spend most of the day ticking invoices against bank statements for clients, then writing up what doesn't match. I share a flat with two girls from my course, and I cook dinner most nights because I like the routine.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that there's a right answer. A number either ties or it doesn't, and my senior, Marguerite, shows me why. What wears me out is the busy season, when we stay until eight and the partners keep adding clients. My dad runs a little pharmacy and he's backing me while I settle in, so I'm not stressed about rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was hype, and everybody can calm down. At work I'd tell Marguerite that the software we have already does enough. I wouldn't post anything online, I don't really do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it still means a bit more pressure on juniors, because the partners will try the new tools on us first. But my job feels safe in this one. I have six months of savings and plenty of firms are hiring in Bristol, so I could move if Hartwell & Pike got silly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am. I'd keep doing my tick-and-tie by hand, because I trust it, and I'd finish my professional exams on the schedule the firm set, which is about two evenings a week. I'd also keep putting a little aside each month, about a third of my pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, if I'm honest. A bit annoyed that people made such a fuss about it, though. I'd go back to worrying about rent going up, which is the thing that really happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be careful about the checking work. Does any of your day change in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little, yes. Some of my day is routine, like matching the same supplier lists every quarter, and the firm has a spreadsheet macro that does part of that now. I do it by hand anyway, and Marguerite lets me because it's quick on small clients. If the macro got better I'd probably be told to use it, and I'd grumble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the firm squeezed juniors even so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The partners, not the software. They'll say it's about efficiency, and then they'll hire fewer graduates and keep the same profits. I'd say the same to my dad. A firm that makes that much money can afford to train people, and I'd want the junior pay scale written down for everyone.

say: I'd say the **hype** was overblown and the old tools were already enough.
I'd tell my senior that **routine** work is fine by hand and quick on small clients.
think: I think my job is **safe** here, and I could move firms if I had to.
I worry the partners will still use new tools as an excuse to **squeeze** juniors.
do: Keep doing **tick-and-tie** by hand and finish my professional exams on schedule.
Save about **a third** of my pay each month and keep it in my current account.
feel: I feel **calm**, with a small annoyance at all the fuss.
S0.quote: A firm that makes that much money can afford to train people, and I'd want the junior pay scale written down for everyone.
fieldNote: Priya is **secure** here: strong savings, many local openings, and a job she understands.
Her anger goes to **partners**, not technology, a pattern that runs through all five answers.
She admits **routine** matching work is already half automated, but she refuses the macro.

steps.text: Keep doing tick-and-tie checks by hand on small clients
Put a third of each month's pay into savings
Ask Marguerite to write the junior pay scale down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's moving faster than the firm admits, and nobody has told us what happens to juniors. I'd probably join the staff chat that the trainees set up and say we should ask for a plan. I'd keep it civil.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the checking I do all day is exactly the work that goes first. Hartwell & Pike takes six graduates a year and I could see that dropping to two. I'd be one of the people the partners compare, and I don't use any of these tools, so I'd look slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start by asking Marguerite what the firm plans and whether the trainees can join a union or a staff group. I'd keep studying for my exams, because a qualification still counts for more than any tool. And I'd put the extra into savings, since I live cheaply and my dad's help gives me room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, mostly, and a bit angry. I worked three years for this degree and it feels like the ladder is being sawn off just as I step onto it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said some of this lands on the checking you do. What does that look like in your office in a year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In a year I think the first-year audits will be run by a tool and checked by one senior. Marguerite would do the judgement, and I'd be the one whose job turned into watching a screen. I'd rather be asked to learn the judgement part than to babysit software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the partners if they asked you to use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm happy to learn it if the firm trains me properly in work time, not at ten at night. I'd ask them to put it in writing that using the tools won't count against my hours target. I know that sounds stubborn, but I don't trust a promise with no paper behind it.

say: I'd tell colleagues the firm should publish a **plan** for graduate hiring.
I'd say trainees should ask for **training** in work time, in writing.
think: Privately, I think the **checking** I do all day is the work that goes first.
I fear the firm takes **fewer** graduates and I look slow because I avoid the tools.
do: Ask Marguerite what the **firm plans** for trainees and join a staff group.
Keep studying for my **exams**, since a qualification outlasts any tool.
Save more of my pay, using my dad's **backing** as a cushion.
feel: I feel **nervous** and angry about the ladder being sawn off.
I also feel a quiet **loyalty** to the work I've just learned.
S1.quote: I worked three years for this degree and it feels like the ladder is being sawn off just as I step onto it.
fieldNote: The first scenario where her own **job** feels at risk: checking work is her daily task.
She wants **collective** protection and written promises, consistent with her left-leaning views.
**Resistance** to tools is a real risk she half-recognises, then defends.

steps.text: Ask Marguerite what the firm plans for graduate trainees
Join the trainee staff group and push for written training time
Pass my professional exams on the firm's schedule
Add half of each pay rise to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's reckless, and governments should step in before it happens. I'd go on a march if there was one, and I'd sign anything asking for income support and rules on firms. I'd say it loudly at work too, even to the partners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my job is gone, or at least the version of it I trained for. Auditing is reading, checking and writing up, which is the thinking work they say comes first in 2028. The robots for hands-on work come three years later, but I don't do hands-on work, so that part doesn't save me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one, I'd talk to my dad and see how long he could back me. I'd stop eating out, cancel the gym and work out how many months of savings I have, which is over six. I'd also go to a union meeting, because a union can ask for severance, and I can't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not panicking, but my stomach feels tight. I'd lie awake doing sums about rent and the exams I've paid for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What would you actually do in the first month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad first, over the phone, and I'd tell him I need him to be honest with me about what the pharmacy can cope with. He'd want to help, and I'd feel guilty. He's already giving up his Sundays to do the stock take himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your life would you tell first, and what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years doesn't give me time to finish my qualification and use it. I'd rather get any job that has people in it, like a care role or the pharmacy counter, than sit and wait. It sounds like a step down, but I'd rather earn than wait.

say: I'd say **governments** must act, with income support and rules on firms.
I'd tell colleagues I'd join a **march** if one was organised.
think: Privately, I think **auditing** is reading and writing up, so my job could be gone by 2028.
Hands-on robots come later, but my work is not **hands-on**, so I get no extra time.
do: Ask my dad how long he could **back** me, then cut gym and eating out.
Count my **savings**, which are over six months, and make a plan.
Go to a **union** meeting to ask for severance terms.
feel: I feel **frightened**, with a tight stomach, and guilty about relying on my dad.
S2.quote: Two years doesn't give me time to finish my qualification and use it.
fieldNote: Strong **cushion** cannot offset her view that her exact tasks vanish quickly.
She turns first to **family** and union, not to retraining.
**Guilt** about her father's pharmacy shows what is at stake emotionally.

steps.text: Ask my dad how long he could back me
Cancel the gym and stop eating out
Go to a union meeting about severance terms
Apply for care work or pharmacy counter jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a little time, so use it, and push for retraining funds and a proper safety net. I'd write to my local MP, which I've never done. I'd say the firm should be open about its plans so people can prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I get a few years of work, but not a full career. I'd be around 27 when it arrives, a senior at best, and the senior roles might hold a bit longer than the first-year ones. So I'm less scared than in the two-year one, but still sure the shape of my job changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my qualification quickly, in about two years, so I've got something solid. I'd save hard, maybe 40 percent of my pay, and I'd look for a second skill, like tax advice for small shops, where people want a human face. And I'd finally try one of the AI tools, probably with a flatmate beside me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Better than the two-year one. It feels like a deadline I can plan around, though it's still a bit like standing at the bottom of a hill that's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years feels different from two. What do you do with those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say save your money and don't panic. My flatmate Chloe works in marketing and she'd say use the tools before they use you. I'd probably roll my eyes and then do it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad and your flatmates say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The difference is I can pick a skill and go with it. In two years I'd just be reacting. With five I'd choose tax advice for small shops, because those customers like someone they can sit across from, and I can make that work.

say: I'd say we should use the time to **retrain** people and fund a safety net.
I'd write to my local **MP**, which I've never done.
think: Privately, I think I get a few years of work, but not a **full career**.
Senior roles may hold longer than first-year ones, so I'm **less scared** than with two years.
do: Finish my **qualification** within two years so I have something solid.
Save around **40 percent** of my pay each month.
Learn a second skill, like **tax advice** for small shops.
feel: I feel **better** than with two years, like I can plan around a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd choose tax advice for small shops, because those customers like someone they can sit across from, and I can make that work.
fieldNote: More **time** lets Priya move from reaction to a plan, but the worry is still there.
She finally considers trying an **AI tool**, but only with a friend beside her.
Her retraining idea is a **human-contact** niche, matching her values.

steps.text: Finish my professional qualification within two years
Save 40 percent of my pay each month
Write to my local MP about retraining funds
Try an AI tool with my flatmate Chloe beside me

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a gift, and we'd be fools not to use it. I'd say schools and employers should start now, with paid retraining and fair rules. I'd probably say it a bit like a speech, because I feel strongly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it means a normal career with a big bend in the middle. I'd work until about thirty-two doing something like my job, then need a second path. I'd be older, maybe with a flat of my own and a partner, so I'd have more to lose but also more savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and finish my exams, then try to move into advising, where the judgement is. I'd also buy a small flat in four or five years with my savings and family help, because owning something feels safe. And I'd learn the tools slowly, one thing a month, so they're not a shock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly okay, to be honest. Ten years is long enough to grow into things, and I'd stop feeling like the ground is shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, what changes about the choices you make this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them to get good at things people want from people: listening, explaining, being trusted. I'd tell them a certificate is not enough by itself. And I'd tell them to expect their job to change twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your own children, if you have them, to know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd spend less time worrying and more time on the qualification, because it still matters in 2030. I'd put money into a flat rather than shares, since I trust bricks more than screens. I'm not saying that's the clever move, it's the one I'd sleep with.

say: I'd say a decade is a **gift** and employers should fund paid retraining.
I'd argue for **fair rules** now, before the change arrives.
think: I think my career gets a big **bend** around thirty-two, then a second path.
With ten years I'd have more to lose but also more **savings**.
do: Finish my exams, then move into **advising** where judgement matters.
Buy a small **flat** in four or five years with savings and family help.
Learn one new **tool** a month so nothing is a shock.
feel: I feel **mostly okay**, because ten years is long enough to grow into change.
S4.quote: I'd tell them to get good at things people want from people: listening, explaining, being trusted.
fieldNote: With a **decade** she relaxes, and her cautious instincts turn to property and qualifications.
She names a **flat** as emotional security, not as a clever investment.
Slowest **tool adoption** of all five scenarios, but she now plans a gradual start.

steps.text: Finish exams, then move toward advising work
Save for a small flat in four years
Learn one new software tool every month
Talk with my dad about helping with a deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year picture, without a doubt. My exams take until next summer, and I'd have no time to turn them into anything. What would help is a firm that says what it will do for its graduates, a union or staff group behind me, and some kind of income support from the government if the work dries up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I know I'm one of the lucky ones. I have savings and my dad behind me, and I still feel scared, so I can't imagine how it feels for someone with debt.

headlineQuote: I have savings and my dad behind me, and I still feel scared, so I can't imagine how it feels for someone with debt.
portrait: Priya, 22, is a **junior auditor** in Bristol who still checks every invoice by hand and avoids AI tools.
She is secure with over six months saved and **family backing** from her dad's pharmacy.
She blames **partners and big firms**, not the technology, and wants written promises and union backing.
Her mood rises from calm in the plateau to **alarmed** with two years, then eases with a decade.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because it leaves no time to finish her exams and use them.
whatWouldHelp: A firm that states its **plan** for graduates, and a union or staff group behind her.
Government **income support** if auditing work dries up.
